body.head: LITERARY
body.p:
The greatest novelty in literature of recent birth here, is an extravagant demonstration of "Young America" in the shape of "Leaves of Grass," by Walter Whitman. It is advertised as poetry, but is little more than lines printed in sentences, instead of paragraphs; and with some remarkable flashes, may be pronounced destitute of both rhyme and reason. A page of it would make Emerson sick of his "transparent eyeball" forever after. It is Emerson run mad in the utmost looseness of the author, whose half-dressed portrait is prefixed; and he strips soul as well as body to the buff. [...]
[...]

p.note: This article begins with recommendations for "our more intelligent readers" of publications from the North American Review and the Christian Examiner.
The article concludes with brief mention of an anticipated reprinting of Leigh Hunt's The Old Court Suburb
